content.text: JavaScript passes every argument by value. For an object, that value is a reference, so the function and the caller share one object: changing its properties shows up outside, but assigning a new object to the parameter only changes the function's own variable. This is called pass by sharing, and real pass by reference doesn't exist in JavaScript.
A product list has a "Clear filters" button. Its handler calls
, which sets the parameter to a fresh copy of the defaults. Nothing happens: no error, and the old filters stay applied. A few files away, a helper that "only reads" the search query adds a default
to it, and the URL suddenly gains a sort order the user never picked. Both bugs come from the same sentence the team believes: "objects are passed by reference".
The belief: primitives are passed by value and objects by reference, so a function that receives an object has full access to the caller's variable, including replacing it with a different object.

Half of it is easy to observe. Change an object's property inside a function and the caller sees the change, which is exactly what "by reference" seems to promise. Tutorials and interview answers repeat the phrase, and "reference" is the right word for what a variable holds when its value is an object. The mistake is in "pass by": what the function receives is a copy of that reference, not access to the caller's variable.
A variable holding an object holds a reference
, the object lives somewhere in memory and

copies the reference, not the object, so you get two variables and one object. Nothing about this is specific to functions yet. Primitives follow the same copy rule; you just can't tell, because a number or a string can't be changed in place, so a copy and a shared value behave the same.
A call copies each argument into a new variable

MDN puts it in one line: arguments are always passed by value and never by reference, and object arguments are passed by sharing. Each parameter is a new local variable, initialized with a copy of the argument's value. For an object, that copy is the same reference, so the function and the caller now share one object. That's
: the object is shared, the variables are not.
Two lines that look alike do very different things.
follows the reference and changes the shared object, so the caller sees it.
points the local variable at a new object, and the caller's variable still points at the old one. In a language with real pass by reference, like a C#
parameter or a C++ reference parameter, the parameter is an alias for the caller's variable, so that reassignment would reach the caller. JavaScript has no equivalent.

Frameworks that detect changes by comparing references, like React state setters and Angular signals, can skip an update when you hand back the same object you just mutated. Meanwhile every other holder of that object sees the change at once. Treat objects you receive as read-only unless the function's name says it mutates.

items.title: Never reassign a parameter to "return" a value

content.text: If a function computes a new object, return it and let the caller assign it. Reassigning a parameter only ever changes the function's own variable.

items.text: JavaScript passes every argument by value; for objects, the value that gets copied is a reference.
The function and the caller share the object, so mutating its properties is visible outside.
Reassigning a parameter only changes the function's local variable; the caller's variable never moves.
and spread don't make objects immutable:
blocks reassignment, and spread copies one level.
To replace what a caller's variable points to, return a new value and let the caller assign it.
